making-good-on-private-duty-practical-hi: Nurse Harriet Camp Lounsbery wrote this hands-on guide for graduate nurses taking on private-duty work in patients' homes. It covers everything from managing difficult households to keeping one's own health and professionalism under strain. Full of practical wisdom from the early 1900s, the book offers a rare look at what nursing was really like before the modern hospital era.
italian-hours: Henry James, the great American novelist, spent decades wandering Italy, and these essays are his love letter to the country. Venice, Rome, Florence, and Naples appear in prose that notices everything — light on old stone, the rhythm of street life, the weight of history. Readers get Italy through the eyes of a master observer at the height of his powers.
the-potiphar-papers: George William Curtis skewers fashionable New York society in these witty satirical sketches from the 1850s. Through the fictional Mrs. Potiphar and her circle, he mocks dinner parties, opera boxes, and the desperate pursuit of status. Light on the surface and sharp underneath, the papers remain a delightful portrait of American high society at its silliest.
on-the-pampas-or-the-young-settlers: G. A. Henty, the king of boys' adventure, plants his young heroes on the vast pampas of Argentina. Cattle ranching, gauchos, and frontier dangers fill a story that taught British boys about the wider world. Henty's blend of excitement and sturdy values made him the favorite author of generations of young readers.
the-coming-of-the-friars: Historian Augustus Jessopp recounts how the Franciscan and Dominican friars arrived in medieval England and changed its religious life. Drawing on chronicles and local records, he shows the friars preaching in towns, founding houses, and stirring the faith of ordinary people. A scholarly yet readable account of a spiritual revolution.
the-caesars: De Quincey turns his formidable learning to the Roman emperors in these brilliant, idiosyncratic essays. From Augustus to the fall of the Western empire, he meditates on power, character, and fate with his trademark ornate eloquence. History as only De Quincey could write it — part scholarship, part prose poetry.
england-under-the-tudors: Arthur Innes surveys the Tudor century — Henry VII to Elizabeth I — when England rose from medieval kingdom to great power. The Reformation, the Spanish Armada, and Shakespeare's age unfold in clear, balanced narrative. A reliable, readable introduction to one of English history's most dramatic periods.
venus-in-furs: Leopold von Sacher-Masoch's famous 1870 novella tells of Severin, who begs the beautiful Wanda to dominate him — and learns the cost of his fantasy. The book that gave masochism its name remains a startling, psychologically acute study of power and desire. A landmark of erotic literature, unsettling and unforgettable.
four-years: W. B. Yeats recalls four formative years in this autobiographical memoir — the Dublin literary world, the Irish revival, and the friendships that shaped him. Written with the poet's memory for atmosphere, it brings fin-de-siècle Ireland vividly alive. Essential for understanding the making of a Nobel laureate.
the-british-association-s-visit-to-montr: Lady Rayleigh's letters describe the British Association's 1884 meeting in Montreal — the scientists, the ceremonies, and the Canadian hosts who welcomed them. Written with a lively eye, they capture a moment when science was fashionable and empire was confident. A charming piece of Victoriana.
the-happy-adventurers: Lydia Miller Middleton's cheerful tale follows young adventurers through escapades designed to delight young readers — small dangers, kind friends, and happy endings. Lighthearted and wholesome, it belongs to the golden age of children's series fiction. Simple pleasures, well told, for bedtime or rainy afternoons.
the-last-of-the-huggermuggers: Christopher Pearse Cranch's droll fantasy brings in the Huggermuggers, kind giants of the deep, in a tale that won young hearts. Among the first storybooks of American fancy, it came before Alice won the nursery. Full of fun, good nature, and pleasing strangeness.
the-pothunters: P. G. Wodehouse's school story follows the pothunters of St. Austin's — boys chasing athletic trophies and the glory that comes with them. Through a term of cricket, rivalry, and mischief, friendships are tested and schoolboy honor upheld. Written before Jeeves made him immortal, the novel already shows the master's effortless comic touch and his affection for the English public school world.
ghosts-i-have-met-and-some-others: Humorist John Kendrick Bangs — the dean of American funny men — meets ghosts with his tongue firmly in cheek in these comic supernatural tales. His spooks are as funny as they are spectral, haunting drawing rooms rather than graveyards. Light, clever entertainment from a master of the droll and the absurd.
across-the-years: Eleanor H. Porter — beloved author of Pollyanna — looks across the years in these warm stories of love, loss, and quiet hope. Her glad philosophy shines through tales meant to comfort and inspire tired hearts. Gentle, old-fashioned fiction from a writer who believed deeply in the goodness of people.
in-the-courts-of-memory-1858-1875-from-c: Lillie de Hegermann-Lindencrone, a Danish singer, recalls the courts of Europe from her letters of 1858 to 1875 — kings, queens, and artists met along the way. Her memories sparkle with gossip and grace. A delightful insider's view of a vanished world.
pages-from-a-journal-with-other-papers: William Hale White, writing as Mark Rutherford, offers pages from a journal — quiet thoughts on faith, doubt, and daily life — with other papers. His plain, honest prose goes straight to the heart. A classic of Victorian inner life. Doubt and faith wrestle quietly in these pages, which have comforted generations of honest seekers.
lives-of-the-necromancers: William Godwin, the radical philosopher, gravely chronicles the lives of necromancers — magicians, alchemists, and wonder-workers from history and legend. His cool, skeptical eye makes the marvels all the stranger. A curious, learned cabinet of magic and imposture. From ancient magi to medieval alchemists, his sober pen makes old wonders walk again.
the-life-of-captain-matthew-flinders: Ernest Scott tells the life of Captain Matthew Flinders — the navigator who charted Australia and gave the continent its name. His voyages, his long French captivity, and his early death make a moving story. The definitive biography of a great explorer.
roman-holidays-and-others: Howells' Roman Holidays — sketches of the Eternal City and other travel pieces — show the American in Europe at his observant best. His quiet humor and clear eye charm and enlighten. Delightful wandering with a wise companion. The Forum, the Campagna, and quiet pensions fill his sketches.
tom-of-the-raiders: Austin Bishop's Tom of the Raiders follows a brave boy among border raiders — a tale of the wild frontier, full of riding and daring. His young hero faces outlaws and Indians with true grit. A rousing Western adventure for boys who love the old frontier days.
the-logbooks-of-the-lady-nelson-with-the: Ida Lee gathers the logbooks of the brig Lady Nelson, with the journal of her first commander, Lieutenant James Grant. These official records trace Australia's early coastal surveys in daily detail. Historians prize them as primary sources of the continent's discovery. Invaluable for all students of Australian exploration.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbreviators: A 1913 entry on the abbreviators — the papal officials who drafted briefs and bulls. Their college was a prized Roman post. P.M.J. Rock explains their work. The Vatican's penmen, in an age of quills. Their signatures filled the papal registers for centuries.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-acts-of-the-m: This 1913 reference piece on the Acts of the Martyrs — the records of the early confessors. James Bridge sifts the genuine from the legendary. Blood wrote the Church's first annals. Faithful unto death, in their own words. Polycarp's letter is the crown of them all. Their courage built the Church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-algiers: This 1913 reference article on Algiers — the archdiocese of French Algeria. Georges Goyau tells its modern rise. Lavigerie's white fathers spread from here. The cathedral faces the blue bay. A frontier church of the Mediterranean. Its white city climbs the hillside.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-angers: A 1913 entry on Angers — the French diocese of Anjou. Georges Goyau gives its history. Its cathedral crowns the Maine. The counts' castle guards the town. A see of the western Loire. Its tapestries show the Apocalypse. Its Plantagenet tombs guard the abbey.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-anglican-orde: This 1913 reference article on Anglican orders — the Catholic judgment of their validity. Sydney Smith explains Apostolicae Curae. Leo XIII declared them null. The bull settled the long debate. Rome's final word on the question. Its verdict closed a century's debate.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-annals-of-the: This 1913 reference piece on the Annals of the Four Masters — Ireland's great chronicle. Douglas Hyde honors its Franciscan compilers. Donegal's friars gathered the old tales. The Gael's history runs unbroken. Erin's memory in manuscript. Their volumes span two thousand years.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-apostolic-exa: This 1913 reference article on the apostolic examiners — the testers of bishops-elect. Andrew Meehan explains their office. Rome probes the chosen shepherds. The Church guards its high offices. The gatekeepers of the episcopate. Their questions test the candidate's learning. Their report goes to the consistory.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-apostolic-exp: This 1913 reference piece on the apostolic expeditors — the agents of the Roman court. Andrew Meehan describes their trade. They sped the bulls through the chancery. The curia's business ran on their feet. The brokers of the papal seals. Their fees were fixed by tariff.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-apostolic-let: This 1913 reference article on apostolic letters — the pope's written instruments. F.M. Rudge sorts their solemn kinds. Bulls, briefs, and encyclicals speak. The Church hears Peter's voice. The paperwork of the papacy. Their seals are lead or gold. Their Latin style is the curia's own.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-assessors: This 1913 reference article on assessors — the advisers of the ecclesiastical judge. William Fanning explains their learned aid. They counsel but do not decide. The tribunals lean on their lore. The judge's council of experts. Their opinions guide the judge's sentence.
